content: Chloroquine phosphate functions as an antimalarial agent. While it has been observed to inhibit certain enzymes, its primary effect is thought to stem, at least partially, from its interaction with DNA. However, the exact mechanism by which chloroquine exerts its plasmodicidal effects remains incompletely understood. Chloroquine demonstrates activity against the erythrocytic stages of Plasmodium vivax, Plasmodium malariae, and chloroquine-susceptible strains of Plasmodium falciparum. However, it is not effective against the gametocyte forms of Plasmodium falciparum or the exoerythrocytic stages of the parasite. Laboratory studies involving Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites have shown that chloroquine also exhibits amebicidal properties, with efficacy comparable to that of emetine. Resistance to chloroquine is widespread among Plasmodium falciparum strains, and there have also been documented cases of resistance in Plasmodium vivax.
